text: Build microdns with cabal, run it locally against the example zone file, and what to set up before running it on UDP port 53.
title: Getting started with microdns

heading: Getting started with microdns
text: microdns serves fixed records from a file and everything else from memory. That is, you configure it after it has started, by calling an HTTP(S) API, and it loses those records if it restarts.
title: Getting started with microdns

heading: Run the example
text: microdns is a Haskell cabal project. From a checkout of the repository: cabal update echo unsafe > secret-web-hmac-file.txt cabal run -- microdns plain \ --dnsPort 5354 --dnsApex example.com. \ --webPort 3333 --webHmacSecretFile secret-web-hmac-file.txt \ --zoneFile fixtures/example.mzone Then, from another terminal: dig +short @127.0.0.1 -p 5354 example.com answers 1.2.3.4, the A record in fixtures/example.mzone. The options are: --dnsPort: the UDP port answering DNS queries. --dnsApex: the delegated DNS apex. --webPort: the TCP port of the configuration API. --webHmacSecretFile: the file holding the shared secret that authenticates dynamic registrations. --zoneFile: the MicroZone file with the fixed records. The tls command takes the same options plus --certFile and --keyFile, and serves the configuration API over HTTPS.
title: Getting started with microdns

heading: Running it for real
text: Unless you have really good reasons not to, run microdns on UDP port 53. You also need to listen on a TCP port of your choice for configuration requests. Use TLS to protect the API calls: the current code is sensitive to replay attacks. The HMAC mechanism is not very strong, so you should probably not expose the configuration API on the Internet if your domain is a sensitive target. For tech-savvy individuals with low-profile blogs, it is probably enough. Assuming some Linux, the best is to run chrooted, with only enough privileges to do networking and read the certificate and HMAC files. Say microdns is installed in /usr/local/bin: you can grant the binary the right to listen on port 53 even for non-root users with Linux capabilities (man 7 capabilities). setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' /usr/local/bin/microdns Also consider rate-limiting incoming and outgoing UDP, as DNS over UDP is prone to abuse. An example rate limit, using netfilter: nft add rule inet filter input udp dport 53 limit rate over 10/second drop

text: The zone-file format microdns reads its fixed records from: the supported record types, the apex syntax, and a commented example.
title: MicroZone files

heading: MicroZone files
text: microdns uses its own zone-file format, with limited support for DNS records: all TTLs are 300, and there is no support for the CHAOS class, for instance. The file is given with --zoneFile and read at startup; see Getting started. An example file, with comments, is as follows. It is the repository’s fixtures/example.mzone. -- comments start with "--" -- all records have fixed TTL to 300 -- there are no wildcards -- the @ special syntax replaces the current apex in some records (from the commandline or overriden) -- otherwise, all domain names are fqdns -- A and AAAA records A example.com. 1.2.3.4 AAAA example.com. ::1.2.3.4 -- TXT wants quoted strings TXT example.com. "microdns has \"quoted\" strings with \\ (backslashes)" TXT @ "apex syntax" -- CAA has two quoted strings CAA example.com. "issue" "letsencrypt" -- MX MX example.com. 10 1.2.3.4 MX example.com. 100 spool.example.com. -- CNAME CNAME dir.example.com. directory.example.com -- SRV have only priority SRV _altweb._tcp.example.com. 10 8080 1.2.3.4 microdns:apex other.example.com. TXT @ "apex syntax in other.example.com." The microdns:apex directive changes the apex that @ stands for in the records that follow it; before any such directive, @ is the apex given on the command line with --dnsApex.
title: MicroZone files

text: The HTTP(S) endpoints that add A, AAAA and TXT records to a running microdns, and the shared-secret HMAC that authenticates them.
title: Dynamic registration

heading: Dynamic registration
text: Records that are not in the MicroZone file are registered while microdns runs, by calling its HTTP(S) API. They are kept in memory and lost on restart. There are only a few registrations available.
title: Dynamic registration

heading: Endpoints
text: Expose the client IP as A (or AAAA for IPv6 clients) for ${subzone}.${apex}, mostly for the dynamic-DNS problem. The client IP is taken from the x-forwarded-for header if present: POST /register/auto/:subzone?apex=:apex Expose A or AAAA records (the syntax follows Net.IPv4.decode and Net.IPv6.decode): POST /register/a/:subzone/:value?apex=:apex POST /register/aaaa/:subzone/:value?apex=:apex Expose TXT ${subzone}.${apex} ${value}, mostly for ACME-challenge tokens: POST /register/txt/:subzone/:value?apex=:apex
title: Dynamic registration

heading: Authentication
text: An HMAC-256 with a shared secret provides a minimum of authentication (see MicroDNS.DynamicRegistration.verifyHmac). Requests carry the header: x-microdns-hmac: ${base16-encode(hmac(${secret_key},${apex}${subzone}))} In its present form, the implementation lacks nonces and only hashes the apex and subzone. Queries that can be spied on can therefore be modified and replayed. As a result, if you use the dynamic-registration API over the Internet, TLS should be mandatory. Note that the apex is the empty string when missing from the URL query parameters: it is not replaced with the one given on the command line. Said another way, the secret key is the only command-line parameter that influences the HMAC.
title: Dynamic registration
